claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs is governed by competition between lattice-distortion-induced local chemical ordering and configurational entropy.
Increasing Al concentration increases lattice distortion in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
The Al-induced lattice distortion arises primarily from differences in atomic radii and bonding.
Increasing Al promotes local chemical ordering and formation of an ordered B2 or BCC-related phase in an otherwise FCC matrix.
Lattice-distortion-induced ordering mediates transformation between disordered FCC and ordered B2/BCC-like structures.
Higher Al content lowers the free-energy barrier for local ordering relative to the disordered FCC state.
The resulting nanoscale ordered regions have coherent, lattice-distorted interfaces.
Nanoscale ordered regions and their coherent interfaces impede dislocation motion.
Nanoscale ordered regions and their interfaces impede radiation-induced defect propagation and improve defect recombination.
Nanoscale ordered regions and their interfaces arrest crack propagation at low temperatures.
Within a critical Al range, increased ordering raises high-temperature yield strength relative to a lower-Al baseline.
Within a critical Al range, increased ordering reduces irradiation-induced swelling or defect density relative to the baseline.
Within a critical Al range, increased ordering reduces oxidation rates and improves environmental resistance.
Within a critical Al range, increased ordering enhances cryogenic toughness.
The lower-Al baseline has a predominantly disordered, nearly single-phase FCC microstructure.
Excessive Al or ordering produces brittle intermetallics and embrittlement rather than beneficial behavior.
The proposed beneficial behavior requires a fine dispersion of local ordering without gross phase separation.
The extent and effects of ordering are sensitive to annealing temperature and time.
